outline.keyPoint: Your child has a subject on the timetable called «Natur und Technik», nature and technology, and may well be growing cress on the windowsill, a common homework in this topic. This video is for parents who do not speak German. In about twelve minutes you learn what the subject is, what the Bavarian curriculum expects in the topic on seed plants, which pictures carry the ideas, the German words your child will use, and how to help with a real experiment at home, even if you cannot read the worksheet.

«Natur und Technik», usually shortened to «NT», is the subject where science begins at a Bavarian Gymnasium. There is no separate biology, physics or chemistry yet; they come later. In Year six, «Jahrgangsstufe sechs», pupils aged eleven to twelve, the subject is mostly biology, with a smaller informatics part. The topic in this video is «Samenpflanzen als Lebewesen», seed plants as living things, planned for about sixteen lessons. It follows a first topic on how scientists work, gaining knowledge, communicating and judging, and puts those methods to use.

In short, the first part of the topic asks pupils to do four things. One: explain how the structure of fruits and seeds serves reproduction and dispersal, and weigh the costs and benefits of different dispersal strategies. Two: compare plant structures with technical products, which the curriculum calls «Bionik», bionics, to see that nature can give engineers ideas. Three: compare sexual reproduction by seeds with asexual reproduction by runners, «Ausläufer», by costs and benefits. Four: conclude from their own experiments how outside factors such as water, light, temperature and oxygen affect germination and growth. The second part, plant parts and photosynthesis, is covered in other videos. Your school's plan may order things differently.

One idea runs through the whole of school biology, and this topic introduces it: structure and function. Every part of a living thing has a shape, and the shape does a job. The question your child learns to ask is: why does it look like this, and what is it for? Three pictures carry that idea here: the seed cut open, the flying fruit, and the three ways a seed can travel. The captions on screen are German, as your child sees them in class.

Idea one: the parts of a seed, «der Same». Cut lengthwise, three parts appear, and the curriculum names exactly these three. The seed coat, «die Samenschale», protects. The food store, «das Nährgewebe», feeds the young plant for its first days; in a bean it sits in the two thick seed leaves, «die Keimblätter», which strictly belong to the embryo; school pictures still show the store as its own part, as here. And the embryo, «der Embryo» or «der Keimling», is the tiny plant itself, with an embryonic root, «die Keimwurzel», and an embryonic shoot, «der Keimspross». The question is not what the parts are called, but what each part is for.

Idea two: the fruit, «die Frucht», is the seed's travel unit. The maple fruit, «die Ahornfrucht», carries its seed in a wing that spins as it falls, like a helicopter blade. Falling slowly gives the wind time to carry it away from the parent tree; the stronger the wind, the further it goes. The dandelion does it differently and floats on a parachute. This is where bionics comes in, «die Bionik», which the curriculum names explicitly: a helicopter rotor uses a similar principle, a rotating wing that creates lift; the maple spins by itself, the helicopter has a motor. Your child should be able to spot such a shared principle between a plant part and a machine and explain why it works in both.

Idea three: dispersal, «die Ausbreitung», compared by costs and benefits. Wind: the dandelion makes very many light fruits with little parachutes; most are wasted, but no animal is needed. Animals that eat: the cherry invests in sweet flesh; birds carry the stone far away and drop it with fertiliser. Animals that carry: the burr, «die Klette», hooks into fur and pays nothing in flesh, but depends on an animal passing by. In every case the whole fruit is the travel unit of the seed. The curriculum asks for exactly this comparison: what does a strategy cost the plant, and what does it gain?

Here are the words in one place, in three groups: the words for the seed and for sprouting, the words for travelling and bionics, and the words for the experiment, which matter beyond this topic because they return in every science lesson for years. You do not need to pronounce them. You need to recognise them when your child says them or when they appear on a worksheet.

The seed is «der Same», plural «die Samen». You will also meet the form «der Samen» in the singular; it is the same word, and in school texts the plural «die Samen» is what you see most. The fruit is «die Frucht». The coat is «die Samenschale», the store «das Nährgewebe», the embryo «der Embryo» or «der Keimling», two words used almost interchangeably, with «Keimling» more common for plants. Its root is «die Keimwurzel», its shoot «der Keimspross». Sprouting is «die Keimung», the verb «keimen». The parent plant is «die Mutterpflanze». «Keim» means a first shoot here; in everyday German it can also mean a germ as in bacteria, and context tells which.

Travelling is «die Ausbreitung», dispersal. «Die Bionik» is bionics, technology inspired by nature. The maple fruit is «die Ahornfrucht», the burr «die Klette», and the Velcro it inspired is «der Klettverschluss». Then the experiment words, which your child will use for years: «die Hypothese», the hypothesis, «die Variable», the one thing you change, «die Konstanten», what stays the same, «der Kontrollversuch», the control experiment, and «das Versuchsprotokoll», the written record of the experiment. These last five are the most valuable words in the whole topic.

A quick check for you. Your child has two dishes of cress on the windowsill, points at the dry one and says: «Das ist mein Kontrollversuch». What is that dish for, and why does the experiment need it? Take a moment. Think about what you would not know if there were only the watered dish.

The dry dish is the control, «der Kontrollversuch». It is treated exactly like the other dish, same seeds, same place, same warmth, except for the one thing being tested, the water. If only the watered dish sprouts, the water was the cause. Without the control, cress sprouting in the watered dish would prove nothing; maybe it would have sprouted dry as well. This is the single most important idea in the scientific method your child is learning, and it is worth a conversation at the windowsill.

The most useful thing you can do at home is the experiment itself. The curriculum wants children to conclude from their own experiments how water, light, temperature and oxygen affect germination, guided by a hypothesis. That sounds big, but cress, cotton wool and two dishes do it in a week. You need no German for this: the method is the same in every language, and your child supplies the German words.

Step one: your child writes down a hypothesis, «die Hypothese»: cress needs water to germinate. Step two: two dishes with cotton wool, the same number of seeds, the same warm, bright place. Step three: only one dish is watered. That single difference is the variable; everything kept the same are the constants; the dry dish is the control. Step four: after three days, count how many seeds have sprouted in each dish and write a short record: question, hypothesis, set-up, observation, conclusion. That record is the «Versuchsprotokoll» the teacher expects.

You do not have to explain anything; you can ask. What did you change, and what did you keep the same? What is the second dish for? What would you not know without it? What would happen if you changed water and light at the same time? Then you could not tell which one caused the result, and that insight is the heart of the method. Finally: was your hypothesis right, and how can you tell? A child who can answer these in any language has understood the method, not just the cress.

Once the first experiment has worked, the other factors follow the same pattern, with one trap worth discussing. Temperature: a fridge is cold and dark, so put both dishes in closed boxes, one box in the fridge and one in the room; then only the temperature differs. Light: one dish under a cardboard box. Oxygen: seeds fully under water instead of on damp cotton wool; the result can be less clear. Always one variable at a time. The light experiment holds a surprise: many seeds, though not all, germinate in the dark, but the seedlings come up pale and tall. Plants need light mainly afterwards, to grow.

Three things parents often ask. Which wrong ideas are common, and how do you spot them? How is this subject assessed, since it works differently from maths and German? And what else is in this topic? The misconceptions are stubborn because they come from everyday life. The assessment is lighter than in the main subjects. And the second half of the topic is harder than the first.

Four misconceptions that appear in many classes. One: fruit and seed are the same thing. The fruit is the packaging, the seed is inside: in an apple the flesh and core are the fruit and the pips are the seeds; in a cherry the seed sits inside the hard stone, which is still part of the fruit. Two: all seeds need light to germinate. Many sprout in the dark underground, though some kinds do need light; all need light afterwards, for growing. Three: a seed is dead. It is resting and waiting for water, warmth and air. Four: the seedling feeds on soil. For its first days it lives on the store inside the seed, and later it makes its own food from light, water and carbon dioxide; it takes water and minerals from the soil, but soil is not its food. Each of these is corrected by a picture or an experiment, not by a rule.

In Year six, «Natur und Technik» is usually one of the subjects without the big written tests called «Schulaufgaben». Grades come from smaller pieces: short unannounced tests, «Stegreifaufgaben», at some schools announced short tests, oral participation, experiment records and sometimes presentations. Typical tasks in this topic: label a seed in section, justify the dispersal strategy of a given fruit, compare costs and benefits, evaluate a germination experiment and explain the control. How exactly your child's school handles this is the teacher's decision; the exercise book and the experiment records show it.

The second half of the topic is more demanding. First the jobs of the plant parts: root, stem and leaf, «Wurzel», «Sprossachse» and «Blatt». Then photosynthesis and respiration, «Photosynthese» and «Zellatmung», simplified to the level of particles, with the idea of converting matter and energy: the plant builds sugar from water and carbon dioxide using light. From that follows why plants matter for food, renewable materials and fossil fuels. Finally, plants respond to their surroundings: they grow towards light and open and close their flowers. Those get their own videos.

In short: this topic teaches three ways of thinking. Structure and function: what is each part of the seed and the fruit for? Costs and benefits: what does a plant invest in its dispersal, and what does it gain? And the experiment with a control: what really caused the result? Ask about these three things at home, grow cress with a «Kontrollversuch», and let your child explain the record to you in any language. The German version of this guide and the lesson for children are on this channel. Subscribe for the next topic.

Animals that carry: the burr, «die Klette», hooks into fur and pays nothing in flesh, but depends on an animal passing by. In every case the whole fruit is the travel unit of the seed. The curriculum asks for exactly this comparison: what does a strategy cost the plant, and what does it gain?
scenes.onScreenTitle: Idea 3: three ways to travel, with costs

scenes.narration: Here are the words in one place, in three groups: the words for the seed and for sprouting, the words for travelling and bionics, and the words for the experiment, which matter beyond this topic because they return in every science lesson for years. You do not need to pronounce them. You need to recognise them when your child says them or when they appear on a worksheet.
scenes.onScreenTitle: The words your child brings home

scenes.narration: The seed is «der Same», plural «die Samen». You will also meet the form «der Samen» in the singular; it is the same word, and in school texts the plural «die Samen» is what you see most. The fruit is «die Frucht». The coat is «die Samenschale», the store «das Nährgewebe», the embryo «der Embryo» or «der Keimling», two words used almost interchangeably, with «Keimling» more common for plants. Its root is «die Keimwurzel», its shoot «der Keimspross». Sprouting is «die Keimung», the verb «keimen». The parent plant is «die Mutterpflanze». «Keim» means a first shoot here; in everyday German it can also mean a germ as in bacteria, and context tells which.
scenes.onScreenTitle: Seed and sprouting words

scenes.narration: Travelling is «die Ausbreitung», dispersal. «Die Bionik» is bionics, technology inspired by nature. The maple fruit is «die Ahornfrucht», the burr «die Klette», and the Velcro it inspired is «der Klettverschluss». Then the experiment words, which your child will use for years: «die Hypothese», the hypothesis, «die Variable», the one thing you change, «die Konstanten», what stays the same, «der Kontrollversuch», the control experiment, and «das Versuchsprotokoll», the written record of the experiment. These last five are the most valuable words in the whole topic.
scenes.onScreenTitle: Travel and experiment words

scenes.narration: A quick check for you. Your child has two dishes of cress on the windowsill, points at the dry one and says: «Das ist mein Kontrollversuch». What is that dish for, and why does the experiment need it? Take a moment. Think about what you would not know if there were only the watered dish.
scenes.onScreenTitle: The words your child brings home

scenes.narration: The dry dish is the control, «der Kontrollversuch». It is treated exactly like the other dish, same seeds, same place, same warmth, except for the one thing being tested, the water. If only the watered dish sprouts, the water was the cause. Without the control, cress sprouting in the watered dish would prove nothing; maybe it would have sprouted dry as well. This is the single most important idea in the scientific method your child is learning, and it is worth a conversation at the windowsill.
scenes.onScreenTitle: The answer

scenes.narration: The most useful thing you can do at home is the experiment itself. The curriculum wants children to conclude from their own experiments how water, light, temperature and oxygen affect germination, guided by a hypothesis. That sounds big, but cress, cotton wool and two dishes do it in a week. You need no German for this: the method is the same in every language, and your child supplies the German words.
scenes.onScreenTitle: The experiment at home

scenes.narration: Step one: your child writes down a hypothesis, «die Hypothese»: cress needs water to germinate. Step two: two dishes with cotton wool, the same number of seeds, the same warm, bright place. Step three: only one dish is watered. That single difference is the variable; everything kept the same are the constants; the dry dish is the control. Step four: after three days, count how many seeds have sprouted in each dish and write a short record: question, hypothesis, set-up, observation, conclusion. That record is the «Versuchsprotokoll» the teacher expects.
scenes.onScreenTitle: The cress experiment, step by step

scenes.narration: You do not have to explain anything; you can ask. What did you change, and what did you keep the same? What is the second dish for? What would you not know without it? What would happen if you changed water and light at the same time? Then you could not tell which one caused the result, and that insight is the heart of the method. Finally: was your hypothesis right, and how can you tell? A child who can answer these in any language has understood the method, not just the cress.
scenes.onScreenTitle: Questions you can ask, in any language

scenes.narration: Once the first experiment has worked, the other factors follow the same pattern, with one trap worth discussing. Temperature: a fridge is cold and dark, so put both dishes in closed boxes, one box in the fridge and one in the room; then only the temperature differs. Light: one dish under a cardboard box. Oxygen: seeds fully under water instead of on damp cotton wool; the result can be less clear. Always one variable at a time. The light experiment holds a surprise: many seeds, though not all, germinate in the dark, but the seedlings come up pale and tall. Plants need light mainly afterwards, to grow.
scenes.onScreenTitle: Further experiments

scenes.narration: Three things parents often ask. Which wrong ideas are common, and how do you spot them? How is this subject assessed, since it works differently from maths and German? And what else is in this topic? The misconceptions are stubborn because they come from everyday life. The assessment is lighter than in the main subjects. And the second half of the topic is harder than the first.
scenes.onScreenTitle: Misconceptions, assessment, and what comes next

scenes.narration: Four misconceptions that appear in many classes. One: fruit and seed are the same thing. The fruit is the packaging, the seed is inside: in an apple the flesh and core are the fruit and the pips are the seeds; in a cherry the seed sits inside the hard stone, which is still part of the fruit. Two: all seeds need light to germinate. Many sprout in the dark underground, though some kinds do need light; all need light afterwards, for growing. Three: a seed is dead. It is resting and waiting for water, warmth and air. Four: the seedling feeds on soil. For its first days it lives on the store inside the seed, and later it makes its own food from light, water and carbon dioxide; it takes water and minerals from the soil, but soil is not its food. Each of these is corrected by a picture or an experiment, not by a rule.
scenes.onScreenTitle: Four common misconceptions

scenes.narration: In Year six, «Natur und Technik» is usually one of the subjects without the big written tests called «Schulaufgaben». Grades come from smaller pieces: short unannounced tests, «Stegreifaufgaben», at some schools announced short tests, oral participation, experiment records and sometimes presentations. Typical tasks in this topic: label a seed in section, justify the dispersal strategy of a given fruit, compare costs and benefits, evaluate a germination experiment and explain the control. How exactly your child's school handles this is the teacher's decision; the exercise book and the experiment records show it.
scenes.onScreenTitle: How this subject is usually assessed

scenes.narration: The second half of the topic is more demanding. First the jobs of the plant parts: root, stem and leaf, «Wurzel», «Sprossachse» and «Blatt». Then photosynthesis and respiration, «Photosynthese» and «Zellatmung», simplified to the level of particles, with the idea of converting matter and energy: the plant builds sugar from water and carbon dioxide using light. From that follows why plants matter for food, renewable materials and fossil fuels. Finally, plants respond to their surroundings: they grow towards light and open and close their flowers. Those get their own videos.
scenes.onScreenTitle: What comes next in this topic

scenes.narration: In short: this topic teaches three ways of thinking. Structure and function: what is each part of the seed and the fruit for? Costs and benefits: what does a plant invest in its dispersal, and what does it gain? And the experiment with a control: what really caused the result? Ask about these three things at home, grow cress with a «Kontrollversuch», and let your child explain the record to you in any language. The German version of this guide and the lesson for children are on this channel. Subscribe for the next topic.

publish.description:
For parents who do not speak German and whose child attends Jahrgangsstufe 6 at a Gymnasium in Bavaria. What the subject Natur und Technik is, what the LehrplanPLUS expects in topic NT6 1.2 Samenpflanzen als Lebewesen, the core ideas in 3D pictures (parts of a seed, the fruit as dispersal unit, dispersal by wind and animals, bionics), the German terms with their English meaning, the cress experiment with a control for home, typical misconceptions and how the subject is assessed.

German terms in this video: Natur und Technik, Same, Frucht, Samenschale, Nährgewebe, Embryo, Keimwurzel, Keimspross, Keimblätter, Ausbreitung, Ahornfrucht, Klette, Bionik, Keimung, Hypothese, Variable, Kontrollversuch, Versuchsprotokoll, Ausläufer, Stegreifaufgabe.

The German version for parents (Eltern-Lektion) and the lesson for children (Lektion) are on this channel as well. Curriculum: LehrplanPLUS Gymnasium Bayern, Natur und Technik 6, Lernbereich 1.2.

Transparency: the narration is a computer-generated voice (text-to-speech). The script follows the Bavarian LehrplanPLUS and was checked by a second AI model; a parent reviews every video before publication.
